newsitem.title: MEXICO: FLUSH WITH CASH, IS MEXICO'S CARSO GOING SHOPPING?
newsitem.headline: FLUSH WITH CASH, IS MEXICO'S CARSO GOING SHOPPING?

text.p: Mexican conglomerate Grupo Carso will be fat with cash in a few months, and already analysts are wondering what the expansion-hungry company will gobble up next.
Carso, Mexico's biggest conglomerate with interests in everything from mining to retail, is set to rake in some $600 million in cash, having sold off chunks of its cigarette and paper subsidiaries.

"Obviously there are a lot of rumors about this, but at this time all we know is that Carso has a lot of cash and a long history of buying up companies," said Robert Hulme, an analyst at Interacciones brokerage in New York.

Carso will get some $400 million for the sale of 21 percent of its cigarette division Cigatam to U.S. tobacco giant Phillip Morris Cos Inc and an additional $170 million from Proctor and Gamble Co for its Loreto y Pena Pobre paper firm.
Carso's billionaire chairman Carlos Slim has made a name for himself in Latin America by forging a small business in tires and cigarettes into a firm with annual sales of more than $3 billion.
Much of the growth has come the same way: buying up troubled companies at bargain prices and turning them around into profitable ventures that turn their former owners green with envy.
His peers call Slim Mexico's modern-day Midas -- turning company rubble into gold.

"The thing to look for now is a potential target -- a mismanaged company that has a price to book value of below one and which is compatible with Carso's businesses," Martin Lara, an analyst at Caspian Research, told Reuters.

Carso went shopping for good value earlier this year, when it doled out $103 million for 60 percent of Sears Roebuck and Co's Mexico subsidiary, which had been hard hit by Mexico's recent recession. Analysts applauded the buy as shrewd and Carso has since upped its stake beyond 80 percent.

The Sears purchase boosted Carso's interest in retail beyond its successful Sanborns chain and it could be looking to add to its weight in that sector, which is expected to recover in the coming two years as real wages begin to rise.

Retail prospects include department store chain Suburbia and the restaurant chain Vip's, both owned by retailer Cifra SA, or troubled retailer Salinas y Rocha, analysts said. "Vip's and Suburbia both have a lot of synergy with Carso's retail portfolio, which has become one of the biggest in Mexico in terms of sales and floor space," said Robert Ford, a retail analyst at Merrill Lynch in New York.

Carso, through its financial group Inbursa, might also up its minority stake in several other businesses, including retailer Gigante and chemicals and plastics firm Cydsa SA. Inbursa has about a 15 percent stake in each.
Other analysts said Carso could buy a stake in Mexican broadcaster TV Azteca, which plans to launch a global initial public offering on Thursday.
"I don't think Carso would mind having a piece of that cake in the least," said one Mexico City analyst, who wished to remain anonymous.
Few analysts expect Carso to use the cash to reduce its debt levels, which they said are manageable at about 22.9 billion pesos.
Carso officials refused comment for this story.
